\title{CredDefer: Capacity-Constrained, Uncertainty-Aware\\
Human Review for Credit Risk Decisions}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Credit-risk systems should not only estimate the probability of default;
they should recognise when their knowledge is insufficient and allocate
scarce human-review capacity accordingly. We study this deferral problem in
CredDefer, a cloud-deployed research prototype evaluated on 307{,}511 real
loan applications. A deployed disagreement-based deferral rule proved
\emph{anti}-selective: it routed the model's most confident cases to human
review, a failure invisible to aggregate metrics that a cheap permutation
audit exposes (no router among 10{,}000 random draws produced a deferred
pile as easy; empirical $p < 10^{-4}$). We diagnose the mechanism, a
near-constant calibration offset between the two scores, and repair it:
uncertainty-based routing reverses the inversion at the mandated 22.5\%
review rate, confirmed on an untouched final split, and epistemic
(knowledge) uncertainty from a single stochastic-gradient-Langevin-boosted
model reaches a random-to-oracle routing position of 0.40 versus 0.14 for
the classical reject-option baseline, without a second model. A cost-aware
study then separates the two objectives a review budget can serve:
epistemic uncertainty finds the cases the model is most likely wrong about,
while expected-loss ranking minimises financial decision cost. A
replication on an independent Taiwanese credit corpus transports the audit
and the single-model machinery while showing that the best-routing
uncertainty component shifts with the base rate, so routing signals must be
re-raced at the operating prior rather than imported. Every supporting
modelling claim was adjudicated by one pre-registered fold-paired criterion
under committed, dated protocols.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
credit risk, learning to defer, human-in-the-loop, uncertainty quantification,
selective prediction, fairness, explainable AI
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
Automated credit assessment concentrates research attention on a single
number, ranking accuracy (AUC), while the institutions that deploy such
models are accountable for an entire \emph{decision process}: which
applications are decided instantly, which are escalated to a human
underwriter, what the applicant is told, and what trail an auditor can
follow. Existing credit-risk systems primarily optimise predictive
discrimination; the operational problem of allocating a \emph{fixed} and
\emph{scarce} human-review capacity according to model uncertainty, and of
verifying that a deployed deferral rule actually does its job, remains
comparatively underexplored in deployed credit decisioning pipelines. In
India this accountability is becoming explicit: the Reserve Bank of India's
Digital Lending Directions~\cite{rbi2025} and its FREE-AI committee report on
responsible AI adoption in the financial sector~\cite{rbifreeai} articulate
expectations of explainable decisions, human oversight of uncertain cases,
and end-to-end auditability.

This paper reports the design and measured evaluation of \textbf{CredDefer},
a human-in-the-loop (HITL) credit decisioning research prototype built and
deployed on 307{,}511 real loan applications from the public Home Credit
corpus~\cite{homecredit}. We organise the work around three research
questions:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{RQ1.} Can a deployed deferral rule be audited cheaply, and can
epistemic uncertainty improve human-review allocation under a fixed deferral
budget?
\item \textbf{RQ2.} Does feature enrichment provide greater predictive
improvement than model fusion or architectural novelty in credit-risk
classification?
\item \textbf{RQ3.} Can domain-constrained monotonicity provide directional
explainability without materially degrading predictive performance?
\end{itemize}

Our contributions, in order of importance:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A permutation audit for deployed deferral rules, and an
inversion it caught (RQ1).} We show that a deployed disagreement-based
deferral rule can be \emph{anti}-selective: ours deferred the model's most
confident cases, a failure invisible to aggregate metrics. The audit costs a
few lines (deferred-pile decision loss against a random-router null), with
10{,}000 permutations resolves empirical $p$-values to $10^{-4}$, and its
findings survive a three-stage split whose final slice no candidate ever saw
(Sec.~\ref{sec:deferral}).
\item \textbf{Single-model epistemic routing (RQ1).} Knowledge uncertainty
from stochastic-gradient Langevin boosting (SGLB) virtual
ensembles~\cite{ustimenko2021,malinin2021} routes review cases to position
0.40 on the random$\to$oracle axis versus 0.14 for the classical
reject-option baseline~\cite{chow1970} at the same 22.5\% rate, approaching
two-model disagreement without a second model; a replication on an
independent Taiwanese credit corpus~\cite{yeh2009} confirms the audit and
the single-model machinery while showing that the best-routing uncertainty
component shifts with the base rate (Sec.~\ref{sec:taiwan}).
\item \textbf{A measured subgroup account of who gets deferred (RQ1).} The
thin-file deferral asymmetry turns out to be a property of the \emph{router},
not of deferral itself: the better-audited uncertainty routers reduce it
substantially, from 3.4$\times$ under the inverted rule to near-flat under
the epistemic signal, although the reduction is not monotonic across all
policies;
we also report the approval, calibration and ranking gaps each policy leaves
across gender, age and region groups, as measurements rather than claims
(Sec.~\ref{sec:fairness}).
\item \textbf{A pre-registered evaluation discipline with dated evidence
(RQ2, RQ3).} Every comparative claim was decided by one rule, fixed in
committed experiment protocols before results existed (commit hashes in the
reproducibility statement): a gain counts only if the fold-paired mean AUC
delta exceeds the measured fold-noise floor. The same rule that rejected our
own hyperparameter tuning later rejected every model fusion we attempted.
Under it, the first feature enrichment cleared the floor for all four
evaluated models in every fold and a second, independent enrichment did so
for both models carried forward, while nothing architectural ever did
(Sec.~\ref{sec:results}); and monotonicity
constraints cost an AUC delta inside the floor while making directional
explanations structural (Sec.~\ref{sec:studies}).
\item \textbf{A reproducible deployment of the whole argument.} API, rule
engine, review queue with reviewer-outcome capture behind a deliberately
closed relearning gate, advisory LLM briefings, and decision provenance
stamps run on commodity cloud infrastructure from a single
infrastructure-as-code definition (Sec.~\ref{sec:deploy}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
\textbf{Learning to defer.} Madras et al.\ framed deferral as joint
optimization of a predictor and a rejector against a downstream
decision-maker~\cite{madras2018}; consistent surrogate losses and multi-expert
extensions followed~\cite{mozannar2020,mao2023}, deferral under congestion
and queueing constraints has been analysed
game-theoretically~\cite{lykouris2024}, and recent work treats the rejector
itself as an uncertain component via conformal
prediction~\cite{fang2026}. Empirical studies of humans
working with erroneous algorithmic scores, notably in the Allegheny County
screening deployment, document both the value and the fragility of human
override behaviour~\cite{dearteaga2020}. Our system adopts the L2D framing
but treats the deferral \emph{budget} as a binding operational constraint (a
fixed underwriter capacity band) and, unlike most of this literature, audits
a deployed rule against a random-router null before trusting it.

\textbf{Uncertainty quantification.} Deep ensembles~\cite{lakshminarayanan2017}
and their efficient single-network counterparts~\cite{mukhoti2023} estimate
epistemic uncertainty; calibration of modern models is itself
fragile~\cite{guo2017}. For gradient-boosted trees, still the strongest model
class on tabular data, SGLB~\cite{ustimenko2021} admits principled virtual
ensembles from a single model~\cite{malinin2021}, the mechanism we adopt for
deferral routing. Conformal prediction supplies distribution-free abstention
triggers~\cite{angelopoulos2023,gibbs2021}; selective classification studies
the resulting risk--coverage trade-off~\cite{geifman2017}, which is the
yardstick we use (Fig.~\ref{fig:riskcov}). Jones et al.\ show selective
classification can \emph{magnify} group disparities~\cite{jones2021},
motivating the subgroup measurement in Sec.~\ref{sec:fairness}.

\textbf{Explainability and recourse.} SHAP~\cite{lundberg2017} and
LIME~\cite{ribeiro2016} dominate instance-level attribution in credit
scoring; counterfactual explanations~\cite{wachter2017} supply recourse.
Attribution instability under small perturbations is a known risk for
auditability. CredDefer complements per-decision SHAP with a structural
guarantee: monotonicity constraints make the \emph{direction} of key
explanations a model property rather than a post-hoc estimate.

\textbf{Tabular foundation models.} TabPFN performs in-context learning for
tabular prediction~\cite{hollmann2025}, extended by the TabPFN-2.5
release~\cite{tabpfn25}; Google's TabFM provides zero-shot tabular
prediction~\cite{tabfm2026}; RealMLP~\cite{holzmuller2024} and
TabICLv2~\cite{qu2026} are strong recent non-boosted baselines. We evaluate
these against tuned gradient boosting~\cite{chen2016,ke2017,prokhorenkova2018}
under one protocol (Sec.~\ref{sec:results}) and find them dominated on this
corpus, with output-licensing terms that independently complicate deployment
for lending decisions.

\section{System Design}\label{sec:system}
Fig.~\ref{fig:arch} shows the decision pipeline. We distinguish four roles
that are often conflated: a \emph{predictive model} estimates default
probability; \emph{CBES}, a transparent rule engine, supplies a domain-policy
score; the \emph{decision layer} combines the two signals under thresholds
and a capacity constraint; and the \emph{explanation layer} (per-decision
SHAP, CBES pillar breakdowns, monotone reason directions) communicates why.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_architecture.pdf}
\caption{The CredDefer pipeline. Two opinions (the calibrated serving model
and the CBES rule engine) are blended; the blend decides instantly outside an
uncertainty band and defers inside it. The serving model is deliberately
simpler than the offline research models of Sec.~\ref{sec:results}; the two
tracks are versioned separately. Every decision carries engine version,
artifact name and a threshold-artifact hash; reviewer outcomes are captured
behind a closed relearning gate with a 3\% exploration arm.}
\label{fig:arch}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Two opinions.} The serving predictive model is a calibrated logistic
regression over a 15-field profile contract (holdout AUC 0.6919); the
contract guarantees the training-time feature derivation is byte-identical to
the live API's. CBES (Credit-Based Evaluation System) is a transparent rule
engine over five weighted pillars (credit 0.35, capacity 0.30, behaviour
0.20, stability 0.10, region 0.05), each pillar passed through a softened
logistic link and the weighted sum calibrated to a probability. Its
standalone AUC is 0.5650 on the full population: it is retained not for
discrimination but because an all-ML pipeline fails two institutional tests
at once: a reviewer cannot argue with a gradient, and a regulator cannot
inspect one. Every pillar sub-score is shown to the reviewer alongside the
decision, so disagreement between the two opinions is itself interpretable: a
high ML score over a weak capacity pillar names the conversation the
underwriter should have. Because CBES also enters the blend below, it is a
(bounded) decision signal, not merely an explanation; Sec.~\ref{sec:studies}
ablates exactly what that costs and buys.

\textbf{Blend and thresholds.} Decisions use
$p = (1-\alpha)\,p_{ml} + \alpha\,p_{cbes}$ with $\alpha = 0.10$ chosen from
a measured cost table on a tuning split, bounding CBES's influence to
$\pm 0.0075$ in probability. The base approve threshold ($t_{base}=0.65$) is
fitted by expected-cost minimisation, never on evaluation data; approve and
reject cutoffs bracket it, and the band between them defers.

\textbf{Capacity-aware deferral.} The deferral rate is a business constraint
(20--25\% underwriter capacity; we operate at 22.5\%), implemented as a
tuning-split quantile of the deferral signal. Section~\ref{sec:deferral}
evaluates \emph{which} signal deserves that budget.

\textbf{Capture without feedback.} Reviewer decisions, reason codes,
self-rated confidence and handling time are captured for governance analyses
(override-rate monitoring in the spirit of model-risk guidance), but no code
path reads them as training labels: a four-condition relearning gate is
evaluated on every inspection and has never opened, and a 3\% exploration arm
preserves the counterfactual labels any future relearning would require. We
treat the \emph{refusal} to close the loop as a design feature against
selective-labels feedback. We emphasise the claim boundary: this is a
deployed human-review \emph{workflow prototype} with reviewer-outcome
capture; no human-subject evaluation of reviewer decision quality has been
conducted, and we make no claim that reviewers decide better with the system.

\textbf{Provenance.} Every decision is stamped with the engine version,
serving-artifact name, and a hash of the threshold artifact, surfaced in the
API, both dashboards, and the audit report.

\section{Evaluation Protocol}\label{sec:protocol}
All experiments share one discipline, fixed in each experiment script's
header and committed before results existed. Data: the Home Credit
application table (307{,}511 rows, 8.07\% default rate, 14.3\% thin-file)
plus its credit-bureau table~\cite{homecredit}.

\textbf{Three evaluation populations, never mixed.} (A)~The \emph{main
benchmark}: 5-fold stratified cross-validation (seed 42) on all 307{,}511
rows, identical folds across every experiment so deltas are fold-paired.
(B)~The \emph{foundation-model population}: 8{,}000 rows joined by applicant
identity with an alignment gate (zero label mismatches; AUC reproduces to
four decimals), on which foundation models and a boosted baseline are
compared like for like. (C)~The \emph{serving evaluation}: the deployed
15-field contract's stratified holdout and the decision artifact built from
out-of-fold predictions. Results tables state their population; numbers from
different populations are never compared directly.

\textbf{Claim rule.} For candidate $B$ and incumbent $A$ evaluated on
identical folds $k = 1,\dots,5$ with per-fold AUCs $a_k^{B}, a_k^{A}$:
\begin{equation}
\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{5}\textstyle\sum_k \big(a_k^{B}-a_k^{A}\big)}_{\text{fold-paired mean delta}} > 0.0036
\quad\text{and, for feature claims,}\quad a_k^{B} > a_k^{A}\;\forall k .
\label{eq:claim}
\end{equation}
The floor $\pm0.0036$ is the observed fold-to-fold AUC standard deviation.
We are explicit about what this rule is and is not: it is a
\emph{pre-registered practical effect-size criterion}, not a significance
test; five folds are not independent experiments. Where a claim matters we
therefore also report paired-bootstrap confidence intervals on out-of-fold
predictions (resampling rows, predictions paired), and we distinguish
``exceeds the practical floor'' from ``statistically distinguishable from
zero'' throughout. These row-level bootstrap intervals are conditional on
the fitted out-of-fold predictions: they quantify evaluation noise given the
trained models, not variability over retraining. Pre-registration is evidenced by dated repository commits
(Sec.~Reproducibility). Policy quantities (thresholds, calibrators, deferral
cutoffs) are fitted on a 50/50 tuning split (seed 20260831) and reported on
the held-out half. We use ROC-AUC as the model criterion because at an 8\%
default rate accuracy is dominated by the class prior (always-approve scores
91.9\%); operating-point metrics are reported only with their threshold
stated. Table~\ref{tab:params} lists every decision-layer quantity and how it
was fitted; none is fitted on evaluation data.

\section{Deferral Quality: Audit, Repair, Routing}\label{sec:deferral}
This section answers RQ1 and carries the paper's central contribution. Four
distinct routing policies appear in this paper; Table~\ref{tab:policies}
fixes their identities once, and every result below names the policy that
produced it.

\midrule

(Sec.~\ref{sec:deferral}-A, Fig.~\ref{fig:auditnull} top) \\
Margin uncertainty $|p_{ml}{-}t|$ & validated, wired behind a flag & the repair
result and its final-test confirmation \\

\subsection{A permutation audit for deployed routers}
The original production rule deferred on raw score disagreement
$|p_{ml}-p_{cbes}| > \delta$. We propose the following audit for any
deployed abstention rule. With $n_d$ deferrals and a deferred-pile statistic
$T$, draw $T_1,\dots,T_m$ from $m$ routers deferring $n_d$ uniformly random
cases and report both the standardised score
\begin{equation}
z \;=\; \frac{T - \bar{T}_{\mathrm{rand}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{rand}}}
\label{eq:audit}
\end{equation}
and the \emph{empirical permutation $p$-value}
$p = (1 + \#\{T_i \text{ at least as extreme}\})/(m+1)$, with the alternative
stated one-sided in the direction under test and a resolution floor of
$1/(m+1)$; a $z$-score alone can be inflated by a small estimated null
standard deviation, so we never report one without its empirical $p$. The
\emph{primary} statistic is the deferred-set decision loss
\begin{equation}
R_{\mathrm{defer}} = \tfrac{1}{|D|}\textstyle\sum_{i \in D}
\ell\big(y_i, \hat{y}_i\big),
\qquad
\ell = \mathbb{1}\big[\hat{y}_i \neq y_i\big],
\label{eq:rdefer}
\end{equation}
where $D$ is the deferred set and $\hat{y}_i$ is the hard decision the
no-deferral engine would have taken at its own operating threshold. A useful
router should \emph{raise} the deferred set's expected decision loss
relative to random routing. One sign convention is used throughout this
paper: the unmodified gate statistic computes the equivalent deferred-pile
accuracy $T = 1 - R_{\mathrm{defer}}$, so the one-sided alternative is
lower-tail, $T < \bar{T}_{\mathrm{rand}}$ (equivalently
$R_{\mathrm{defer}} > R_{\mathrm{rand}}$), every reported $z$ is
Eq.~\eqref{eq:audit} evaluated on $T$, and a useful router has
\emph{negative} $z$ with a lower-tail permutation $p$. An anti-selective
router (an easier-than-random pile) has positive $z$; its $p$ is then
computed in the upper tail and marked ``inv.'' wherever it appears. We
report the kept-set loss $R_{\mathrm{auto}}$ alongside $T$, because a router
must both hand humans harder cases and leave safer automated decisions. The
deferred pile's class-balance distance is reported as a supplementary
diagnostic only (a balanced pile is not necessarily a hard one), and because
0/1 loss weights errors equally at an 8\% default rate, every audit is
accompanied by cost-weighted metrics (default recall among deferred cases and
expected decision cost of the auto pile under the stated cost model).
The original audit, run with $m=200$ at the rule's historical
operating point (it deferred 51.8\% of cases), scored $z \approx +28$: the
deferred pile was far \emph{easier} than random. Reconstructed at the
matched 22.5\% capacity rate and re-audited with $m = 10{,}000$, the
disagreement rule scores $z = +36.0$ with \emph{no} random router among
10{,}000 producing a pile as easy (empirical $p < 10^{-4}$ in the inverted
direction), and it routes \emph{fewer} defaulters to review than random
deferral would (16.5\% vs.\ the 22.5\% random expectation): the rule was
systematically sending the model's most confident cases to humans.
Fig.~\ref{fig:auditnull} shows both null distributions and observed values.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_audit_null.pdf}
\caption{The audit of Eq.~\eqref{eq:audit} with $m=10{,}000$ random routers,
both routers at the matched 22.5\% rate. Top: the disagreement router's
deferred pile is far \emph{easier} than any random draw (inverted). Bottom:
the repaired uncertainty router's pile is far \emph{harder} than any random
draw. Neither observed value is reachable by chance at the $10^{-4}$
resolution.}
\label{fig:auditnull}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Diagnosis: disagreement measured calibration, not difficulty}
Measured on the full out-of-fold population, the two scores differ by a
near-constant calibration offset: mean $p_{ml} - p_{cbes} = +0.307$,
positive on 98.4\% of rows, and removing the constant offset shrinks the
mean disagreement magnitude by roughly two thirds. The residual correlates
\emph{positively} with model confidence ($r = 0.38$), so thresholding
$|p_{ml}-p_{cbes}|$ preferentially defers confident cases. The lesson
generalises: a disagreement signal between two differently calibrated scores
measures their scales before it measures difficulty.

\subsection{Repair: racing candidate signals at matched capacity}
We raced candidate signals at the mandated 22.5\% rate, all thresholds
fitted on the tuning half only, all audited on the held-out half by the
unmodified gate statistic with $m=10{,}000$
(Table~\ref{tab:audit}). Three observations. First, repairing the
disagreement signal's scale problem (rank, z-score, or isotonic
normalisation before differencing) fixes the sign ($z$ from $-34.5$ to
$-98.6$); the wired fix, plain model uncertainty (distance of $p_{ml}$ from
the operating threshold), reverses the inversion to $z = -59.7$ (empirical
$p < 10^{-4}$) and lowers the expected cost of the auto-decided pile from
0.0731 (no deferral) to 0.0484 per applicant under the stated cost model
(false approval 0.45, false rejection 0.2644, the constants of the
$t_{base}$ study~\cite{verbraken2014}). The result is stable across
tune/test re-splits ($z = -59.7 / -58.8 / -63.1$ over three split seeds,
each at its permutation floor). Second, the difficulty and cost criteria
rank the variants differently: the $|p_{ml}-0.5|$ variant posts the extreme
$z$ and the highest defaulter capture (57.3\%) because, with nearly all
scores above 0.5, it reduces to deferring the lowest-scoring band, a
\emph{risk ordering} rather than a decision-boundary uncertainty signal; we
report it but do not deploy it, since it largely defers cases the engine
would auto-reject. Third, the audit also scores the currently deployed
artifact policy (deferral on the blended score's uncertainty band at
capacity) as near-random at isolating difficulty ($z = -0.9$, $p = 0.19$):
it satisfies the capacity constraint and is no longer inverted, but
difficulty-targeted signals do strictly better, which is exactly the
decision the audit exists to inform.

Two cost models coexist in this project by design and must not be conflated:
the \emph{decision-layer} pair used throughout this section (false approval
0.45, the Basel II F-IRB supervisory LGD; false rejection 0.2644, the
EMP-measure return parameter~\cite{verbraken2014}; ratio $\approx$1.70) and
the \emph{training study's} pair of Sec.~\ref{sec:studies} (0.75 LGD vs.\
0.10 forgone margin; ratio 7.5), each carried with its provenance. A
sensitivity sweep recomputing Table~\ref{tab:audit}'s cost column under both
pairs and ratios 2--20 finds the qualitative conclusions invariant: the
disagreement rule is last or next-to-last under \emph{every} cost
assumption, and the wired margin rule is in the top three everywhere (first
at ratios $\geq$10); which uncertainty \emph{variant} is cheapest does
depend on the assumed loss ratio, with risk-ordering variants winning only
when false approvals are cheap, so we report the ranking per assumption
rather than a single winner.

\subsection{A selection-bias-free confirmation}\label{sec:finaltest}
Racing six candidates and quoting the winner's statistics from the same
held-out half uses that half for model selection. We therefore repeated the
exercise under a three-stage design: 50\% TUNE (all signal fitting and
thresholds), 25\% SELECTION (the race, with the winner picked by a rule
fixed before results: highest deferred-pile loss, Eq.~\eqref{eq:rdefer},
inside the rate band), and an untouched 25\% FINAL slice evaluated once.
The selection slice picks the $|p_{ml}{-}0.5|$ variant, and the final slice
confirms it: $z = -186.3$, empirical $p < 10^{-4}$, 56.8\% of the slice's
defaulters routed to review, auto-pile cost 0.0253 versus 0.0729 with no
deferral. The production-wired margin rule constitutes a second
\emph{pre-specified} router on this slice (it was fixed by a dated commit
before the present decision artifact existed), and it also confirms:
$z = -42.7$, $p < 10^{-4}$, cost 0.0482. The deployed band policy remains
near-random here too ($z = -0.5$, $p = 0.30$). The audit's findings
therefore survive a split that the candidates never saw.

\subsection{Routing on epistemic uncertainty}
Beyond the repair, we evaluated \emph{epistemic} uncertainty from a single
SGLB-trained CatBoost (posterior-sampling mode; $K{=}10$ virtual
ensembles~\cite{ustimenko2021,malinin2021}). SGLB's Langevin noise makes the
boosting trajectory sample from a posterior over ensembles, so truncating one
trained model at staggered iteration counts yields $K$ approximate posterior
members without training $K$ models. With member probabilities
$p_1,\dots,p_K$ and $\bar{p} = \tfrac{1}{K}\sum_k p_k$,
\begin{equation}
\underbrace{\mathcal{H}(\bar{p})}_{\text{total}} \;=\;
\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{K}\textstyle\sum_k \mathcal{H}(p_k)}_{\text{data (aleatoric)}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{know}}}_{\text{knowledge (epistemic)}} ,
\label{eq:decomp}
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{H}$ is binary entropy and the residual mutual information
$\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{know}}$ is the deferral signal. At an 8\% base rate
nearly all predictions sit below $0.5$, making total and data entropy
near-monotone in $\bar{p}$ itself (correlation 0.94); knowledge uncertainty
is the only component not reducible to the score (correlation $-0.36$ with
the reject-option signal), which is precisely why it carries routing
information the reject-option rule cannot see. We summarise routing quality
by the normalised random$\to$oracle position
$(R_{\mathrm{rand}} - R_{\mathrm{sel}})/(R_{\mathrm{rand}} -
R_{\mathrm{oracle}})$, where $R_{\mathrm{sel}}$ is the kept-pile selective
risk, $R_{\mathrm{rand}}$ the overall error rate (what a random router
leaves), and $R_{\mathrm{oracle}}$ the best achievable kept-pile risk when
the $n_d$ actual errors are deferred first. At the matched rate on the
test half (Fig.~\ref{fig:riskcov}), knowledge uncertainty reached position
0.40 versus 0.14 for the reject-option
baseline~\cite{chow1970} (selective risk 0.217 vs.\ 0.271; random 0.299),
and approached a two-model disagreement signal (0.47) \emph{without a second
model}. It is also higher on thin-file applicants, as an epistemic signal
should be. These comparisons are within one dataset, one calibration regime
and one operating rate; establishing the effect's generality requires
replication on an independent corpus, which we leave as explicit future
work. In the serving frame, the regenerated decision artifact currently
defers on the blended score's uncertainty band at capacity (the near-random
row of Table~\ref{tab:audit}); the measured uncertainty rule is wired behind
a versioned flag, and switching the live routing signal, including any
promotion of the SGLB signal, is an explicitly versioned governance
decision rather than a silent change.

\textbf{Is the uncertainty estimate informative?} Beyond routing rank, the
signal should predict error. Binned by tune-split deciles of knowledge
uncertainty, the test-half decision-error rate rises monotonically from
5.0\% in the lowest decile to 64.7\% in the highest
(Fig.~\ref{fig:deciles}; error-detection AUROC 0.749, AUPRC in the
machine-readable report), against an overall error rate of 29.9\%. The
reject-option margin, scored as an error detector in the same way, sits
below chance (AUROC 0.462) because at this base rate its smallest margins
concentrate in the risky band the engine already rejects.

\textbf{Is the result an artifact of $K{=}10$ or one training run?} No.
Across $K \in \{5, 10, 20, 50\}$ virtual ensembles and three training-seed
sets (twelve configurations, each retrained under the full protocol), the
random$\to$oracle position stays within 0.37--0.40 and the OOF AUC within
0.7745--0.7750. One honest nuance: within a seed the per-case uncertainty
ranks are insensitive to $K$ (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.99$ against the
reference run), but across training seeds they correlate at
$\rho \approx 0.68$, so individual routing decisions are moderately
run-dependent even though aggregate routing quality is not; a production
promotion should average uncertainties over seeds.

\subsection{Is uncertainty the right allocation objective?}
\label{sec:costaware}
Uncertainty is not financial risk: a model can be uncertain about an
economically small case and confidently wrong about an expensive one. We
therefore raced routing \emph{objectives} across a review-capacity grid
(Fig.~\ref{fig:frontier}), under the same three-stage discipline as
Sec.~\ref{sec:finaltest} (tune fits, selection picks, final evaluated once):
random; the reject-option margin; knowledge uncertainty; expected decision
cost $\mathbb{E}[L_i] = p_i c_{FA}$ for auto-approvals and
$(1-p_i)c_{FR}$ for auto-rejections; and a rank-blend
$\lambda\,\mathrm{rank}(U^{epi}_i) + (1-\lambda)\,\mathrm{rank}(\mathbb{E}[L_i])$
with $\lambda$ chosen on the selection slice. The result is a clean negative
for our own headline signal \emph{on this criterion}: the selection slice
chooses $\lambda^{*} = 0$, i.e.\ pure expected-cost ranking, which at the
22.5\% operating rate leaves an auto-pile cost of 0.0314 per applicant
(95\% CI $[0.0308, 0.0320]$) versus 0.0479 for knowledge uncertainty,
0.0583 for the margin rule and 0.0831 with no deferral; blending epistemic
uncertainty into the cost ranking adds nothing. Together with
Fig.~\ref{fig:riskcov}, the honest summary is that \emph{uncertainty and
economic risk are different routing objectives}: epistemic uncertainty buys
error isolation and information-targeted review, expected-loss ranking buys
cost reduction, and an institution should pick (and audit) the objective it
actually holds its review capacity for. The frontier excludes the cost of
review itself; the report carries a per-review-cost grid so total cost can
be read off at any assumed underwriting cost. The result is wired, not only
reported: the serving engine exposes expected-loss routing as a third
flag-gated deferral mode, calibrated in the serving frame under the same
tune/test discipline (at the matched 22.5\% rate the auto-pile cost falls
$0.0731 \to 0.0291$ per auto-decided applicant and 42.0\% of defaulters
reach review, versus 24.7\% under the wired margin rule), with the default
router unchanged pending the policy choice above.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_cost_frontier.pdf}
\caption{Expected auto-pile cost per applicant versus review capacity
(final slice, touched once per strategy; shaded bands are 95\%
row-bootstrap CIs; decision-layer costs 0.45/0.2644). Expected-cost ranking
dominates on this criterion and the $\lambda^{*}{=}0$ blend coincides with
it; epistemic uncertainty wins on error isolation
(Fig.~\ref{fig:riskcov}), not on cost.}
\label{fig:frontier}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Who gets deferred: a subgroup measurement}\label{sec:fairness}
Selective prediction can magnify group disparities~\cite{jones2021}, so a
deferral paper owes a subgroup account. We joined the \emph{deployed band
policy's} decision artifact to applicant attributes (gender, age, region
rating, bureau-file status) and measured the policy's decision mix, ranking
and calibration per group (Fig.~\ref{fig:fairness}). On attribute inputs we
are precise: gender and age enter no component of the decision pipeline;
region is \emph{not} in the 15-field ML serving contract but does enter
CBES's lowest-weight pillar (region, weight 0.05), so a bounded region
influence (at most $\alpha \times 0.05$ of the blend) is present in every
blended decision, and an engineered region$\times$income feature exists in
the offline research models only. Three observations on the deployed policy.
First, review concentrates where information is missing: thin-file
applicants (no bureau record, 14.3\% of the population) are deferred at
34.3\% versus 20.5\% for documented applicants; their auto-reject rate,
however, is also higher (39.0\% vs.\ 20.3\%), tracking their higher observed
default rate (10.1\% vs.\ 7.7\%). Deferral therefore moderates, but does not
remove, the thin-file approval gap. Second, decision-mix gaps across gender
(approval 59.1\% F vs.\ 45.7\% M) and age (36.7\% under 30 vs.\ 68.7\% over
60) track the groups' observed default rates (7.0\% vs.\ 10.1\%; 11.5\%
vs.\ 4.9\%) rather than deferral asymmetries (deferral rates stay within
22.1--25.2\% across these groups); we report them as measurements, not as a
conditional-fairness analysis, which would require controls we do not claim.
Third, calibration is tight in every group with $n \ge 500$ (10-bin ECE
between 0.0011 and 0.0042) and ranking AUC spans 0.719--0.768, lowest for
the oldest and youngest bands.

\textbf{Does the asymmetry depend on the router?} Strongly, and in an
instructive direction (Table~\ref{tab:subrouting}): the better-audited
routers substantially reduce the thin-file deferral asymmetry, although the
reduction is not monotonic across all policies. The inverted historical
rule concentrated review on thin-file applicants at 3.4$\times$ the
documented rate while capturing only 10.9\% of documented defaulters; the
deployed band policy (1.7$\times$) carries a larger asymmetry than a random
router (1.0$\times$) despite being the better deferral policy; the margin
rule reduces it to 1.4$\times$; and the epistemic
router is nearly flat across groups (24.4\% vs.\ 22.4\%) while giving
thin-file applicants the highest default recall of any serving-frame-
comparable policy. The 34.3\% headline is thus a property of the deployed
band policy's calibration geometry, not of epistemic uncertainty, whose
thin-file signal is only slightly elevated. Whether extra thin-file review
\emph{helps} those applicants depends on reviewer behaviour we have not
measured; what we can say is that the better-audited routers send humans
harder cases without singling out thin-file applicants. This is a
descriptive measurement of policies, not a regulatory fairness assessment.

\subsection{Stress tests: does the signal notice shift?}\label{sec:shift}
We subjected one SGLB model (trained on a 60\% slice, thresholds from a 20\%
validation slice) to controlled corruptions of the remaining test slice,
labelled explicitly as synthetic stress tests, not evidence of real-world
generalisation. The monitoring quantity is free: the deferral rate at the
\emph{clean-fitted} knowledge threshold, which a stable system should hold
near 22.5\%. Under information loss (all external-score and bureau-derived
columns masked for a random half of rows), the rate fires to 56.6\% while
AUC falls $0.779 \to 0.720$ and 10-bin ECE rises $0.004 \to 0.053$: the
epistemic signal detects exactly the shift it is supposed to detect. Under
feature noise (Gaussian, half a standard deviation, on 20\% of numeric
columns) accuracy is almost untouched (AUC 0.776) yet the rate still fires
to 38.4\%: the signal detects \emph{distributional} change even when error
does not yet move. On the real thin-file subpopulation the rate is mildly
elevated (24.9\%). One honest negative: under a pure class-prior shift
(default rate doubled by subsampling) ranking is invariant (AUC 0.779) and
calibration degrades sharply (ECE 0.070), but knowledge uncertainty barely
fires (24.6\%); prior shift is a blind spot of the epistemic signal and
belongs to calibration monitoring instead. In every scenario,
knowledge-routed deferral at the matched 22.5\% rate kept selective risk
below the scenario's overall error rate; deferral keeps protecting under
every shift we imposed.

\subsection{An independent-dataset replication}\label{sec:taiwan}
External validity cannot be argued from one corpus, so we replicated the
deferral layer end to end on the UCI Taiwan credit-card default
dataset~\cite{yeh2009} (30{,}000 real customers, 22.1\% default rate):
same fold seeds, same SGLB budget, same tune/test discipline, and the
\emph{unmodified} Home Credit audit code running on the new data. The
replication both confirms and sharpens the claim. It confirms the
machinery: SGLB trains well (OOF AUC 0.7807), every uncertainty router
beats random at the matched 22.5\% rate with the audit at its permutation
floor (empirical $p < 10^{-4}$ for all three signals), and the knowledge
deciles remain monotone in error (16.3\% to 34.9\%). It sharpens the signal
choice: at Taiwan's 22\% base rate the random$\to$oracle ordering flips,
with \emph{total} uncertainty dominating (position 0.415) over the
reject-option margin (0.186) and knowledge uncertainty (0.097). The
mechanism is the one Sec.~\ref{sec:deferral} already identified: at an 8\%
prior, total entropy is near-reducible to the score and knowledge is the
only non-redundant component; at a 22\% prior that reduction no longer
holds, and total uncertainty becomes both informative and non-trivial.
The portable conclusion is therefore procedural, and we state it as such:
\emph{race candidate uncertainty signals at your own operating prior and
audit the winner}; importing a routing signal untested, ours included, is
exactly the failure mode the audit exists to catch.

\section{Supporting Result: Where Accuracy Lives}\label{sec:results}
This section answers RQ2 and explains why the deferral layer, rather than a
better classifier, is where this system's decision quality improves.

\subsection{Features versus fusion}
We held models, folds, and metric fixed and changed only the features: v1,
the original $\sim$113-column numeric frame; v2, 319 engineered columns
adding domain ratios (payment burden, credit-to-annuity term proxy),
external-score combinations, and 35 deep aggregates of the full
credit-bureau table. Fig.~\ref{fig:folddeltas} shows the result:
\emph{all twenty} fold deltas are positive and every model's mean gain is at
least four times the noise floor; a paired bootstrap on pooled out-of-fold
predictions confirms the gains are statistically distinguishable from zero
(CatBoost $+0.0114$, 95\% CI $[0.0104, 0.0125]$; every model's CI excludes
zero). The bootstrap's v1 baseline is the original production
cross-validation run, a slightly stronger baseline than this experiment's v1
protocol, which is why its point estimate is smaller than the fold-paired
$+0.0155$; both baselines are reported so neither can be mistaken for the
other. The best honest fusion of the improved models (a simple
average of the three boosted ensembles) gains $+0.0016$: real in direction
(paired bootstrap CI $[0.0010, 0.0021]$) but below the practical claim
floor. Out-of-fold correlations among the improved models remain 0.87--0.96:
better features made every model better \emph{in the same way}. Separately,
a 14-configuration hyperparameter sweep over the boosted ensembles improved
the early-stopped default by $+0.001$, under a third of the floor, and the
capacity-adaptive learning curve (Fig.~\ref{fig:learning}) still rises at
full data ($+0.010$ AUC per doubling): optimisation is converged,
information is not.

The information explanation then made a confirmable prediction: the four
credit-history side tables not yet used (previous applications, instalment
payments, point-of-sale and credit-card balances) should move the metric
that nothing architectural could. A second pre-registered enrichment, 26
per-applicant aggregates designed from domain knowledge before training
(late-payment shares and magnitudes, refused-application share, revolving
utilisation, minimum-payment shortfalls), was judged by the identical rule
against the recorded v2 fold AUCs: CatBoost gained a fold-paired $+0.0111$
and XGBoost $+0.0104$, every fold positive, both claims granted
(Table~\ref{tab:main}). Cumulatively, feature work moved the best model
$0.7603 \to 0.7868$ while every model change and fusion attempted over the
same period stayed inside the noise floor.

\subsection{Foundation models and 2026 challengers}
Table~\ref{tab:fm} compares foundation models on population B: 8{,}000 rows
joined by applicant identity with an alignment gate (zero label mismatches;
AUC reproduces to four decimals), a safeguard added after an early
row-misalignment incident that we recommend as standard practice for
foundation-model comparisons. Both trail the boosted baseline \emph{on the
same rows}; both fusions die under the floor, and averaging with TabFM
actively hurts (CI $[-0.022, -0.007]$) despite TabFM being the most
decorrelated partner we ever tested ($\rho = 0.66$). Diversity obtained by
being wrong does not cancel errors. Among 2026 challengers screened under
the same rules (30k subsample, defaults only, advance on positive
fold-paired delta), the benchmark-tuned RealMLP~\cite{holzmuller2024} lost
every fold to CatBoost ($-0.0121$ fold-paired), and
TabICLv2~\cite{qu2026} could not complete the screen on commodity hardware
(its in-context inference required $\sim$18\,GB of offload scratch per
fold), a deployability result in itself. Licensing narrows the field
further: the TabPFN-2.5 model card restricts commercial and production use
of its model \emph{outputs} under its licence~\cite{tabpfn25}; we evaluated
checkpoint \texttt{tabpfn\_2\_5} for research comparison only and our
deployment screens prioritised permissively licensed challengers. We state
this precisely for the evaluated checkpoint rather than for every TabPFN
version.

\section{The Decision Layer, Ablated and Priced}\label{sec:studies}
This section answers RQ3 and prices the decision-layer choices.

\textbf{Ablating CBES.} Because CBES is a decision signal and not only an
explanation layer (alone it ranks poorly, AUC 0.5621), we report the
\emph{full decision mix} the blend changes on the held-out half of
population C, both configurations at the matched review rate
(Table~\ref{tab:ablation}). The blend costs discrimination ($-0.0056$ AUC,
paired-bootstrap CI $[-0.0067, -0.0045]$, statistically real) and raises
rejected-or-deferred default capture from 75.1\% to 79.5\%. The
decomposition shows where that capture comes from: the blend converts
3{,}094 false approvals into 2{,}545 at the price of raising false
rejections from 26{,}967 to 28{,}314 (rejection rate 21.9\% $\to$ 23.1\%),
while default recall inside the deferred pile is nearly unchanged (21.6\%
$\to$ 22.0\%). Part of the capture gain is therefore \emph{rejecting more},
not reviewing better, and the net expected cost depends on the assumed loss
ratio: under the decision-layer pair (0.45/0.2644) the blend is slightly
\emph{costlier} per auto-decided applicant (0.0724 vs.\ 0.0716), while
under the 7.5:1 training pair it is cheaper (0.0398 vs.\ 0.0422). We state
this as a measured decision-policy trade-off, not an unqualified
improvement in decision quality; which side of it a lender should take is a
policy choice over the loss ratio, now priced.

\textbf{Monotonicity costs nothing measurable (RQ3).} We fixed 21 sign
constraints from domain knowledge only (external credit scores decrease
risk; payment burden, bureau overdues, leverage and prolongations increase
it; demographic fields deliberately unconstrained) and re-trained the best
model under them. Fold-paired cost: $-0.0008$ AUC, inside the pre-registered
practical floor, with zero direction violations in 14{,}400 empirical sweep
checks. We state the guarantee's scope precisely: the constraint holds by
model construction for each listed feature \emph{with the other inputs held
fixed}; the 14{,}400 checks are sampled verification of that construction,
not an exhaustive proof over the feature space. Within that scope,
directional adverse-action explanations (``your bureau score improved, so
your risk decreased'') become \emph{model properties}, which post-hoc
attribution alone cannot guarantee.

\textbf{Cost-sensitivity belongs in the decision layer.} With a stated
7.5:1 false-negative:false-positive cost model (unsecured-retail
loss-given-default vs.\ forgone margin), class-weighted \emph{training}
never beat cost-optimal \emph{thresholding} of the unweighted model (test
cost delta $+0.000087$ per applicant; paired-bootstrap CI spans zero; the
weighted arm loses at four of five decision-time cost ratios), an empirical
confirmation of Elkan's analysis~\cite{elkan2001} that justifies keeping the
economics in auditable decision policy rather than inside the model.

\section{Deployment as a Research Prototype}\label{sec:deploy}
CredDefer runs as a containerised cloud-deployed research prototype (FastAPI
backend, React front-end, model baked into the image) on commodity
infrastructure defined end-to-end in Terraform: one small instance, a
managed PostgreSQL database in private subnets reachable only through
security-group chaining, and a container registry pulled via instance roles.
The full stack rebuilds from nothing in $\sim$15 minutes and destroys to
zero cost; the demonstration database seeds itself with a committed
510-customer sample spanning instant-approve, instant-reject and defer
outcomes. It is a prototype: no lending institution operates it, and claims
about institutional adoption are out of scope. The TabPFN-2.5 second
opinion, whose checkpoint and in-context set exceed commodity GPU memory, is
served from a free cloud GPU behind an authenticated tunnel and consumed
strictly as advisory input; a \emph{connection run} validates the remote
endpoint by scoring 400 locally-held labelled rows the remote never saw
through four ordered gates (configured; reachable; scores returned for every
row; sane, i.e.\ recomputed AUC clears 0.60; last run 0.710), so a mis-wired
tunnel fails loudly rather than silently. An LLM reviewer briefing
(provider-pluggable) summarises each deferred case from its decision report
under three hard boundaries: advisory only, optional by construction (absent
credentials degrade to an instructive 503), and grounded in the report with
cited fields. On the full population the engine's decision mix is 167{,}751
instant approvals, 70{,}593 instant rejections and 69{,}167 deferrals
(22.5\%); the deployed demonstration routes reviewer adjudications
(including rejections of deferred cases with written reason codes) through
the same capture path, so the review workflow is exercised end to end rather
than mocked. Operational lessons: cache governance endpoints that recompute
from large artifacts; treat boot-script changes as instance replacements;
audit free-tier platform restrictions before capacity planning.

(Table~\ref{tab:rbi}). This is a technical alignment mapping produced by the
authors; it does not constitute a regulatory compliance assessment, and
implementing these mechanisms does not make a system ``RBI-compliant.''

Explainability & SHAP per decision; CBES pillar breakdown; 21 monotone signs
(directional reasons by construction) & monotonicity report: $-0.0008$ AUC,
0/14{,}400 violations \\
Human oversight & capacity-aware deferral (22.5\%); reviewer capture with
reason codes, confidence, time; override monitoring & deferral audit of
Table~\ref{tab:audit}: measured repair, empirical $p < 10^{-4}$ \\
Auditability & engine version + artifact + threshold hash on every decision;
all numbers regenerate from committed scripts & provenance stamps in API,
dashboards, audit report \\
Model governance & versioned research/serving separation; relearning gate
closed; 3\% exploration arm & gate evaluation on every inspection \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

We state one caveat openly: TabPFN-2.5's measured interval on population B
($0.7284 \pm 0.0127$, 8{,}000 engineered-feature rows,
Table~\ref{tab:fm}) sits well above the deliberately feature-constrained
serving model's 0.6919, which is measured on a different population and
feature frame (the 15-field contract's own holdout), so the two numbers
bound a gap rather than form a direct comparison; TabPFN nevertheless
remains advisory because of its output licence, its GPU footprint, and the
governance rule that advisory AI never writes decisions. The roadmap is to
promote the engineered-feature gradient-boosted model, which beats TabPFN-2.5
on identical rows, behind the same serve-time contract.

\section{Discussion: What Generalises}
Five practices from this project transfer beyond credit scoring. First, the
\emph{deferral audit} of Eq.~\eqref{eq:audit} costs a few lines and no new
data, yet it caught a production router doing the opposite of its job; any
deployed abstention rule deserves it, reported with empirical $p$-values
rather than $z$-scores alone. Second, \emph{pre-registration with a
symmetric floor} changed the sociology of our own development: because the
rule in Eq.~\eqref{eq:claim} rejected our tuning gains before it rejected
anyone else's fusion, negative results became reportable rather than
embarrassing. Third, \emph{measure who gets deferred}: deferral policies
have subgroup footprints (Fig.~\ref{fig:fairness}) and assuming they are
benign is not the same as measuring them. Fourth, \emph{licence-aware
challenger selection}: benchmark rank is not deployability, and for
regulated decisioning the licence of a model's \emph{outputs} is as binding
as its accuracy. Fifth, \emph{serve-time contracts}: freezing the feature
derivation shared by training and serving cost us headline accuracy (0.6919
deployed vs.\ 0.7868 offline) but bought byte-identical provenance; the
right response is to promote richer features \emph{through} the contract,
never around it.

\section{Limitations}
Our primary results come from one dataset (Home Credit; Indian-market cost
and regulatory framing over non-Indian data), and the corpus carries no
timestamps, so real temporal shift is untestable here (the stress tests of
Sec.~\ref{sec:shift} are controlled synthetic corruptions). The
independent-dataset replication (Sec.~\ref{sec:taiwan}) covers the deferral
layer only; the feature, serving and subgroup results remain single-corpus,
and it showed the routing-signal choice to be base-rate dependent, so no
fixed signal should be transported without re-racing it. The serving/research accuracy gap (0.6919 vs.\
0.7868) reflects a deliberate 15-field serve-time contract not yet extended
to the engineered features; the two numbers come from different populations
and feature frames and are never compared as models. Deferral findings are
reported in two operating frames (serving and research) whose baselines
differ, and the SGLB routing result, while pre-registered, awaits production
promotion. The human-review workflow is a deployed prototype with outcome
capture; we conducted no human-subject evaluation, so claims about
human-AI complementarity are explicitly out of scope. The subgroup analysis
is descriptive, not causal or conditional. The committed demonstration
sample under-represents the extreme-risk tail (corrected by appending
identity-verified reject-tail applicants), and the relearning loop is
deliberately unproven because it is deliberately closed. All cost
conclusions are conditional on the stated cost pairs (both carried with
provenance, with a ratio sensitivity reported); the three-stage final slice
comes from the same corpus, so it removes selection bias but not
single-dataset risk; and per-case epistemic ranks vary across training
seeds ($\rho \approx 0.68$) even though aggregate routing quality does not.

\section{Conclusion}
Treating the decision pipeline, rather than the classifier, as the research
object yielded reproducible findings a leaderboard cannot express: deferral
rules can silently invert, can be audited with a cheap permutation test, and
the audit's findings survive an untouched final split; a single boosted
model can supply epistemic routing without an ensemble, robustly across
ensemble sizes and training seeds; uncertainty and economic risk are
different routing objectives, and expected-loss ranking, not uncertainty,
minimises decision cost at fixed capacity; the subgroup footprint of
deferral is a property of the router, shrinking to near-flat under the
epistemic signal; accuracy headroom on this corpus lives in information
rather than architecture; and a regulator-relevant explainability guarantee
can be had at a cost inside the practical noise floor. The deferral layer
replicates on an independent corpus, where the audit transports and the
best uncertainty component shifts with the base rate: the procedure, not
the signal, is the portable artifact. Future work: full-system replication
(features, serving, subgroups) on an independent portfolio; temporal and
recency-windowed aggregates of the credit-history tables (the global
aggregates of v3 leave trend information unused); promotion of the
engineered-feature model behind the serving contract; and a human-subject
evaluation of the review workflow.

\section*{Reproducibility}
All experiments are committed scripts writing machine-readable reports;
every number above traces to one. Pre-registration is evidenced by dated
commits: the features-versus-fusion protocol (commit \texttt{8bd7cbf},
2026-09-23), the three model-modification studies (\texttt{4a7cb4c},
2026-09-30) and the deferral race (\texttt{0a253bd}, 2026-08-31) were
committed with their claim rules in the script headers before results were
generated. The revision studies (the 10{,}000-permutation audit, the
three-stage final-test split, the SGLB robustness sweep, the cost-aware
routing comparison and the subgroup routing comparison) are likewise
committed scripts whose selection rules are stated in their headers and
whose outputs are machine-readable reports. Code, infrastructure definitions, figure generators,
machine-readable reports, dependency versions and seeds are prepared for
release as an anonymised archive; the Home Credit licence does not permit
redistributing derived row-level data, so the archive ships regeneration
scripts for all artifacts instead of the artifacts themselves.
